Free relationships tools

20 short exercises on relationships, 2 to 8 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • What you value most in closeness

    Choose and rank the five things that matter most to you in a close relationship. Knowing your own list makes it easier to see when it is being met.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • One relationship, five dials

    Think of one important relationship and set a dial for trust, ease, honesty, reciprocity, and closeness. It works for a partner, a friend, or a family member.

    Dials · 4 min

  • How you show up in conflict

    Rate how often a set of conflict habits has been true for you: going quiet, getting loud, fixing, fleeing, keeping score.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Your conflict moves

    Sort a list of things people do during disagreements into what you do often, sometimes, and rarely. Then look at what your "often" list has in common.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • From frustration to a clear ask

    Take one frustration with someone close to you and work it into a need and a request they could actually say yes to.

    Guided writing · 7 min

  • An appreciation inventory

    Write down what you appreciate about one person in your life, specifically enough that it could only be about them. Then decide whether to tell them.

    Guided writing · 6 min

  • Your support circle

    Place the people in your life on a grid of how close they feel against how much you actually lean on them. The gaps are often revealing.

    Grid · 6 min

  • Repair after conflict

    Turn over cards showing what people often want to say after a fight on one side and what tends to reach the other person on the other.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • When a friendship is drifting

    Think of one friend you have felt further from lately and tick the small signs of drift you recognize. Drift is quiet, and naming it early is most of the work of stopping it.

    Noticing list · 4 min

  • Where your relationship effort goes

    Divide 100 points across the people in your life to show where your effort actually lands: the messages, the visits, the remembering, the showing up.

    Budget · 4 min

  • When you actually talk

    Mark the times in your week when you and the person you live with have a real conversation, not logistics or a screen between you. Most couples and roommates find the map is emptier than they assumed.

    Week map · 3 min

  • How to help me when I am struggling

    Rank the ways people try to help from most to least useful for you. Then you have a list you could actually hand to a partner, friend, or family member.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • Seven days of contact

    Each evening, rate how connected you felt to other people, how much you reached out, and how much others reached you. By the weekend, the three lines start to explain each other.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • Keeping friendships alive

    Build a small, realistic routine for the friendships that matter to you: the low-effort touches, the rituals, and what you do when one of you is struggling.

    Plan builder · 6 min

  • Before you hit send

    A short exercise for the message you are about to send in a heated moment, whether to a partner, a group chat, or a coworker. Five minutes between the draft and the send button.

    Guided exercise · 6 min

  • When they go quiet

    Turn over the stories your mind writes when someone does not reply, cancels, or goes distant, and see the other explanations and the question you could ask instead.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • The invisible load at home

    Place the jobs that keep a home running on a grid of who mostly does them against how visible they are. For couples and roommates, the bottom corners are where the arguments come from.

    Grid · 6 min

  • The roles you play with people

    Choose the parts you tend to play in your relationships: the planner, the listener, the fixer, the one who fades. Then look at which ones you chose and which ones were handed to you.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • The conversation you keep putting off

    Write your way toward a conversation with a family member or someone close that you have been avoiding. Not to rehearse a speech, but to find out what you actually want from it.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • What you say to coworkers, and what you swallow

    Sort things people could say to a coworker into what you say readily, what you say eventually, and what you never say. The last column is where work relationships get stuck.

    Sorter · 5 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
